nameStory: The 'Blue-green Volcanito' gets its dramatic name from its distinctive appearance - tiny crater-like structures that look like miniature volcanoes dotting the lichen's surface. The blue-green coloration comes from the algae living within the lichen, creating an otherworldly landscape that early lichenologists thought resembled volcanic terrain in miniature.
description: Blue-green Volcanito is a crusty lichen that forms thin, spreading patches on tree bark and rocks. This composite organism is made up of fungi and algae living together, with the algae providing the characteristic blue-green tint. The lichen typically spreads in irregular patches up to several inches across, creating what looks like a painted crust with tiny raised bumps scattered across its surface.

idTips.label: Crater-like structures
idTips.description: Look for tiny raised bumps with dark centers that resemble miniature volcanic craters - these are the spore-producing structures that feel slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Blue-green coloration
idTips.description: The overall color ranges from pale blue-green to gray-green, most vivid when damp, becoming duller and more gray when dry

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Surface feels like rough sandpaper or dried paint, firmly attached to its growing surface and difficult to peel off

idTips.label: Irregular patches
idTips.description: Forms spreading, map-like patches with wavy or lobed edges rather than perfect circles

idTips.label: Bark preference
idTips.description: Most commonly found on smooth to moderately rough bark, avoiding deeply furrowed surfaces

habitat: Blue-green Volcanito grows on the bark of deciduous trees and occasionally on smooth rock surfaces in New England's forests. It prefers trees with relatively smooth bark like maples, birches, and young oaks, typically found at eye level or higher on the trunk. Look for it in mature forests with good air quality, as it's sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after spring rains when the blue-green coloration becomes vivid and the lichen appears fresh and well-hydrated.
seasonality.summer: Colors may fade to more gray-green during dry periods, but the distinctive crater-like structures remain clearly visible for identification.
seasonality.fall: Often shows renewed growth and brighter coloration with increased moisture, making it easier to spot against autumn bark colors.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round on bare deciduous trees, though colors are typically more muted and gray during cold, dry periods.

funFact: **Note: Information about this extremely rare lichen species is limited, and some details may be uncertain due to very few documented observations in New England.** Blue-green Volcanito can actually 'resurrect' itself - it can completely dry out and appear dead for months, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet, with its colors returning as if by magic.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other blue-green crusty lichens, but the distinctive raised 'volcano' structures with dark centers are unique - most other crusty lichens have either flat surfaces or different types of bumpy textures that lack the crater-like appearance.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, this is an exceptionally rare find that would be significant to document. If you think you've found this species, consider photographing it and reporting to local naturalist groups, as it may represent an important range extension or rare population.
compareHints: Since no other Megalospora species are documented in our New England dataset, compare it with other crusty lichens in the region. Blue-green Volcanito differs from most crusty lichens by having more pronounced raised structures and a distinctive blue-green cast rather than the grays, yellows, or whites typical of many bark lichens. **Note: Given the rarity of this species, expert confirmation would be valuable for any suspected sightings.**
